transcript_body:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-11
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CTO, Nimbus Health), Daniel Kim (Lead Engineer), Sofia Alvarez (Product Manager)

Summary: quick interactive demo of Hosted API for chat/text generation, focusing on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and retry/backoff strategies to meet Nimbus Health's latency SLOs while optimizing cost. Discussed private deployment concerns, data retention, and next steps for a short pilot.

Topics covered:
- streaming chunk behavior and partial results
- param tradeoffs: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
- retry strategies & backoff (exponential, jitter)
- concurrency / token throughput and cost implications
- console quick tour: token breakdown and latency histogram
- pilot/runbook suggestions

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava: Alright everyone, thanks for joining—I'm Ava with Redwood Inference, AE on the account, uh Marcus is our SE today. quick reminder this call is a demo and Q&A, we'll go through live playground, params, and then look at tradeoffs for latency vs cost.
[00:17] Priya: Great thanks. We're mostly interested in a hosted approach for now, but we want the numbers—like 95th pct latency under 300ms for our triage chat, and obviously cost needs to be reasonable.
[00:28] Marcus: Yep. That makes sense. We'll demo the streaming path, show how partial tokens arrive, and then show config knobs to push latency down or reduce token spend.
[00:40] Daniel: Quick logistics question — we have data residency concerns, but for this initial pilot we can use hosted in us-west. We may need VPC later.
[00:48] Ava: Totally, we can do hosted us-west for pilot and later discuss Redwood Private with VPC/locked control plane.
[00:55] Marcus: Okay jumping in — opening the console sandbox. I'm going to demo a short prompt that simulates a patient triage microconversation. Watch the streaming window — you'll see every chunk as it's generated.
[01:12] [console noise / screen share described]
[01:25] Marcus: Here we triggered chat.generations with model x-rl3 (note: name is approximate in demo), temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9, max_tokens 128. You can see initial token emitted within ~45ms in this environment — that's cold-start-ish though.
[01:40] Priya: 45ms? that's pretty good. is that including network overhead?
[01:44] Marcus: This is the runtime only; from our cloud where the model is hosted to your local network will add another ~20–40ms depending on region. The important piece is streaming latency — first token and then subsequent deltas.
[01:55] Sofia: if we reduce temperature to 0.0 will it be deterministic and faster?
[02:00] Marcus: Temperature is about randomness not speed. lower temp reduces variation in responses, not token generation rate. But smaller max_tokens or stronger stop sequences reduces total generation time and cost.
[02:12] Daniel: Ok, so what are the big levers we should think about to hit 95th pct <300ms?
[02:18] Marcus: Several. One, use a smaller context or shorter history for triage flows to reduce KV cache size and per-token compute. Two, pin to a lower-latency model variant; Redwood has compatible lower-latency quantized variants. Three, tune batch sizes and concurrency: we can reserve dedicated capacity if you need consistent tail latencies. Four, aggressive caching for repeated prefixes — Redwood Optimize suggests prefix caching if you have templated prompts.
[02:44] Priya: You said quantized variants — what's typical perf gain there?
[02:48] Marcus: We often see 1.5–3x throughput improvement with int8/4-bit kernels depending on model and hardware. there's a small accuracy delta; Redwood Optimize can run evals on your prompts and estimate quality impact.
[02:59] [03:00] Marcus: Now about retries — we'll demonstrate two common patterns: client-side exponential backoff with jitter and server-side automatic retries for idempotent requests.
[03:10] Ava: Also worth mentioning that streaming retries differ: for partial responses we recommend checkpoint semantics in the client — either replay from last confirmed token or start a fresh request and dedupe based on request ID.
[03:22] Daniel: Does Redwood provide request ids or resume tokens?
[03:25] Marcus: Yes, responses include a request_id and each chunk has an offset. we also support idempotency keys so you can safely retry without double-appending. sometimes the transcript shows different naming, the console shows a "req_id" field.
[03:39] Priya: Any gotchas with streaming reconnects — if a user loses mobile connectivity for 3–4s and comes back, what's best practice?
[03:46] Marcus: For intermittent drops, we recommend client does optimistic local buffering and on reconnect requests the client can ask server for the last committed token offset using the request_id. If that's not possible, start a new request with the prior conversation state; Redwood's dedupe + conversation id pattern prevents doubling up.
[04:05] Sofia: ok that's useful. Could we see a simulated reconnect?
[04:08] Marcus: Sure — I'll throttle the stream in the sandbox to simulate a slow connection.
[04:20] [sandbox: simulated latency spikes]
[04:35] Marcus: You can see partial chunks stalled, then resumed. The SDK has on_partial callback so you can render incremental tokens. On reconnect we either resume or re-issue depending on how long the gap is.
[04:48] Daniel: What's Redwood's default timeout and max retries?
[04:52] Ava: Default SDK tries 3 client-side attempts with exponential backoff (200ms, 600ms, 1.8s with jitter) for transient 5xx/errors. For streaming we limit automatic retries to cases where the runtime signals safe to resume. For non-idempotent flows we recommend manual retry logic.
[05:12] Priya: And what about concurrency? how many concurrent streams per API key?
[05:16] Marcus: Hosted default is soft-limits based on plan — dozens of concurrent streams on standard, but if you need predictable concurrency we recommend Dedicated. We can show the console quota panel.
[05:28] [05:30] Marcus: switching to the console cost view — here you can see token-level breakdown, cost per 1k tokens, and a latency histogram. For this sandbox run average token latency is ~12ms but tail at 95th is around 280ms in this warm box.
[05:47] Priya: Does the latency histogram include prefix caching effects?
[05:50] Marcus: It does — the console tags calls where prefix cache hit occurred, you'll see them clustered at lower latencies.
[05:58] Daniel: How do we configure caching? automatic or explicit?
[06:02] Marcus: Redwood has automatic prefix/KV caching heuristics; you can also set explicit cache keys if you want deterministic caching for certain templates. Optimize can recommend keys based on pattern analysis.
[06:14] Priya: Let's talk about cost — if we push to keep latency low by reserving Dedicated, what's a rough delta vs hosted?
[06:21] Ava: Dedicated is priced as reserved GPU pools; if you have steady high QPS it is usually cheaper per-token at scale due to utilization. Hosted is better for variable workloads. We'll share a simple breakeven worksheet in the follow-ups.
[06:35] Sofia: Any notes on safety filters and streaming? we have PHI concerns for health data.
[06:40] Marcus: Redwood supports redaction hooks and server-side filters that can be applied before tokens are emitted; for PHI we recommend an additional content filter pipeline in your app or Private deployment with KMS controls. We'll include our SOC2/HIPAA posture in the docs.
[06:55] Priya: Good — send that please. Also, we want to limit retention to 30 days during pilot.
[07:00] Ava: We can set retention at the org level for hosted pilots; Private has more granular retention controls. I'll include options in the follow-up.
[07:06] Daniel: Back to technical — when you mention "batching" how does that affect latency for single user interactive chat?
[07:12] Marcus: Continuous batching dynamically groups requests to improve GPU utilization. For single interactive user the batch sizes are small so latency is minimally impacted, but at moderate concurrency it amortizes overhead. There's a tradeoff: larger batch windows can increase queuing delay. You can configure target batch latency in the runtime.
[07:30] Priya: Can we set the queueing latency target?
[07:33] Marcus: Yes, in Dedicated you can set target_batch_latency_ms and Redwood will tune the runtime. In Hosted we provide conservative defaults but Optimize may suggest lowering target windows for your workload.
[07:44] Sofia: Any examples of real numbers? like if we go from 10ms target to 30ms what changes?
[07:49] Marcus: You'll see higher throughput and lower per-token cost, but tail latency might rise a bit. In some customers we saw 20–40% per-token cost improvement when allowing 20–30ms batching windows.
[08:02] Daniel: Ok makes sense.
[08:06] [08:10] Marcus: Now I'm going to show a few parameter experiments — same prompt, different temperature & top_p, and then we'll time-to-first-token and total tokens.
[08:22] [Demo running experiments]
[08:35] Marcus: With temperature 0.0 top_p 1.0 result is deterministic. token stream arrives similar speed. With temperature 0.8 you get more verbose completions which increases total tokens and cost.
[08:48] Priya: So to optimize cost we should enforce max_tokens and use stop sequences aggressively?
[08:54] Marcus: Exactly. Also use prompt templates that encourage shorter replies. And token compression strategies for embeddings/messages.
[09:02] Daniel: Does Redwood expose per-request cost estimate before executing?
[09:06] Marcus: We have an estimate API that can approximate token count and cost for a payload; it's not perfect but useful for budgeting. We'll include example calls.
[09:15] Priya: Great. A question on retries and duplicates — if a retry occurs after a partial chunk was sent to client, won't the user see duplicate text?
[09:23] Marcus: That depends. If you use idempotency keys + request_id dedupe on server, and your client merges by offset, you can render without duplicates. If not, you'll need to handle de-duplication client-side using the request_id offsets. Some SDKs offer helpers for that.
[09:38] Sofia: Are the SDKs open-source? we prefer to audit them.
[09:41] Ava: Yes, our JS and Python clients are public, link in follow-up. Marcus will point to the exact repos.
[09:48] Daniel: Security — SSO and SCIM provisioning?
[09:52] Ava: We support SAML/SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, RBAC roles, and org-level audit logs. SOC2 compliance is in place; for HIPAA we recommend private deployments and a BAA — we can detail options.
[10:05] Priya: If we do pilot hosted, can we get audit logs sent to our SIEM?
[10:09] Marcus: Yes logs can be forwarded via a configurable endpoint; we also provide log exports in the console.
[10:16] [10:20] Marcus: back to streaming resiliency — here's a sample code snippet I pasted into the chat: it shows exponential backoff with jitter and a logic branch to resume vs restart based on last_chunk_offset. note the pseudo names may be slighly off in transcription.
[10:36] Priya: Good. Could you provide this snippet in Python and mobile-friendly JS?
[10:40] Marcus: Yes will include both in the follow-up.
[10:45] Daniel: About monitoring — what metrics do we get out of the box?
[10:48] Marcus: Tokens in/out, latency percentiles, model variant, cache hit/miss, request_id, error rates, concurrency, per-route cost. You can stream these to your telemetry or view in Console.
[10:59] Priya: For the pilot we want to capture 99th pct as well. Is that exposed?
[11:03] Marcus: Yes, console shows 50/90/95/99 histograms. We recommend correlating traces with request_id to debug tail cases.
[11:12] Sofia: Any example of tail causes?
[11:15] Marcus: Usually queueing due to batching, cache miss causing full KV expansion, or cold model spin-up. Also occasionally network egress spikes. We have auto-warm heuristics to mitigate cold starts.
[11:28] Daniel: If we want sustained sub-200ms 95th, likely Dedicated?
[11:31] Marcus: Often yes — Dedicated with pinned quantized variant plus tuned batch latency tends to give the most predictable tails. But we can run a short lab on hosted first.
[11:41] Priya: Ok. That lab — what data do you need from us?
[11:45] Marcus: Sample traffic traces (anonymized), target percentiles, representative prompts and conversation lengths, and peak QPS windows. We'll use those to configure a 2–3 hour run and produce a report.
[11:55] Ava: We'll also include pricing estimates and a simple ROI breakeven based on expected monthly tokens.
[12:02] Sofia: Timeline — we want pilot done before end of month. is that possible?
[12:06] Ava: Yes if we get traces by 11/14 we can schedule a lab next week and have results by 11/20.
[12:13] Priya: Sounds good. one more quick question — is model versioning supported if we want to test two model families simultaneously?
[12:18] Marcus: Yes, you can pin model versions per-route and run canary traffic split, A/B, and automatic fallbacks. Console shows rollout dashboards.
[12:27] [12:30] Priya: Perfect. thanks.
[12:33] Ava: quick recap — redwood will: send SOC2/SSO docs, sample SDK snippets (py/js mobile), quick pilot pricing, and schedule lab after they provide traces. Nimbus will: share sample traces and latency targets.
[12:46] Priya: We'll send the traces. thanks for the clear demo.
[12:50] Ava: any final questions?
[12:52] Daniel: none from me.
[12:54] Sofia: all good.
[12:56] Ava: great, we'll follow up by email. thanks everyone.

End of meeting.
